videos.title: What is a Call Option? - Free Stock Options Trading Course for Beginners
videos.description:
What is a Call Option?

A call option pays out when the stock price exceeds the strike price on Maturity Date.
• Payout: The option pays the difference between the stock price and the strike price, minus the premium paid.

Example:
• Strike Price = $100
• Stock Price at Expiration = $128
• Payout = $128 - $100 - Premium Paid

• Payout when stock price is higher than strike price: 
If the stock price is below the strike price, the call option expires worthless.

• The premium (the cost of the option when you buy it) is the maximum loss.

• Implied volatility (explained in the Option Q&A in the App - video to come) is crucial in options pricing. Higher volatility increases premiums, making options more expensive.

• Volatility vs. Stock Movement: 
If the stock price goes up but volatility drops, the value of a call option might decrease.
This is because lower volatility limits the potential for larger price moves, reducing the upside.

• Tip: Sometimes it’s better to wait a few hours after market open when volatility is lower, as this can lead to cheaper premiums and more potential upside for calls.

videos.title: What is a Put Option? - Stock Options for Beginners
videos.description:
A put option pays out when the stock price falls below the strike price at expiration.

• Payout: The option pays the difference between the strike price and the stock price, minus the premium paid (which is the cost of the option when you buy it).

Example:
• Strike Price = $100
• Stock Price at Expiration = $80
• Payout = ($100 - $80) - Premium Paid

• Payout when stock price is lower than the strike price: If the stock price is above the strike price, the put option expires worthless.

• The premium (the cost of the option when you buy it) is the maximum loss.

• Implied volatility (explained in the Option Q&A) is crucial in options pricing. 
Higher volatility increases premiums, making options more expensive.

• Volatility vs. Stock Movement: If the stock price goes up but volatility drops, the value of a call option might decrease. This is because lower volatility limits the potential for larger price moves, reducing the upside.

This relationship ensures arbitrage-free pricing and highlights how puts prices and calls prices are interconnected with stock price.

videos.title: Delta of a Call - Stock Options for Beginners
videos.description:
Delta: A Key Metric for Options Trading

Delta measures the sensitivity of an option’s price to changes in the price of the underlying asset. It’s expressed as a number between -1 and 1 (or sometimes as a percentage, -100% to 100%). Here’s what it tells you:

• For Call Options: Delta is positive, ranging from 0 to 1. A delta of 0.50 means the option price is expected to increase by $0.50 for every $1 increase in the underlying asset’s price.

• For Put Options: Delta is negative, ranging from 0 to -1. A delta of -0.30 means the option price is expected to decrease by $0.30 for every $1 increase in the underlying asset.

Why Delta Matters:

1. Directional Sensitivity: Delta shows how much an option’s value will change based on the stock’s price movement.

2. Probability Indicator: For at-the-money options, delta approximates the probability of the option finishing in the money at expiration.

3. Hedging Tool: Traders use delta to hedge positions. For example, owning a call with a delta of 0.50 means holding that option is equivalent to holding 50 shares of the stock.

Examples:

• A deep in-the-money call may have a delta close to 1, reflecting a strong likelihood of it being profitable at expiration.

• A deep out-of-the-money put may have a delta near -0.01, indicating minimal sensitivity to stock price changes.

videos.title: Gamma of a Call - Stock Options Trading Course for Beginners
videos.description:
Gamma: Understanding the Acceleration of Delta

Gamma measures how much an option’s Delta changes in response to price movements of the underlying asset. It reflects the rate of change of Delta and is crucial for managing option positions, especially for hedging.

• Positive Gamma: Both long calls and long puts have positive Gamma. This means Delta increases as the stock price rises and decreases as the stock price falls.

• Negative Gamma: Short positions in options (calls or puts) have negative Gamma, leading to Delta changes that work against the position as the stock price moves.

Why Gamma Matters

1. Delta Stability: Gamma determines how stable Delta is. Higher Gamma means Delta changes quickly with price movements, making it critical for active traders.

2. Risk Management: Understanding Gamma helps traders anticipate large swings in Delta and adjust their positions accordingly.

3. Volatility Impact: Gamma is higher for at-the-money options nearing expiration, reflecting increased sensitivity to price changes.

Examples

• High Gamma: An at-the-money call nearing expiration has high Gamma, meaning its Delta can shift rapidly as the stock price moves.

• Low Gamma: A deep in-the-money or far out-of-the-money option has low Gamma, indicating a relatively stable Delta.

videos.title: Delta and Gamma of Put Options - Stock Options Trading Course for Beginners
videos.description:
Delta and Gamma for Put Options: Exploring Similarities and Differences

When analyzing put options, Delta and Gamma are essential metrics that provide insights into how the option price behaves as the underlying stock price changes. While they are interrelated, each serves a unique purpose.

Delta for Put Options

Delta measures how much the price of a put option changes with a $1 change in the underlying stock price. For puts, Delta is always negative, as the value of a put increases when the stock price decreases.

For example:
• A Delta of -0.40 means the option price decreases by $0.40 for every $1 increase in the stock price.

Delta also indicates the probability of a put finishing in the money.

At-the-money puts typically have a Delta close to -0.50, while deep in-the-money puts approach -1, and out-of-the-money puts near 0.

Gamma for Put Options

Gamma measures how much Delta changes as the stock price moves. It reflects the acceleration of price sensitivity, showing how quickly the Delta of a put adjusts to fluctuations in the underlying asset.

For example:

• A Gamma of 0.05 means Delta will shift by 0.05 for every $1 move in the stock price.

Unlike Delta, Gamma is always positive, as it describes the rate of change in sensitivity, regardless of whether the stock price rises or falls.

How Delta and Gamma Are Similar

Both Delta and Gamma gauge an option’s sensitivity to stock price changes. 

They are highest for at-the-money puts and decrease for deep in-the-money or out-of-the-money options.

Together, they provide a detailed view of how a put option reacts to the stock price and how its sensitivity evolves over time.

Key Differences Between Delta and Gamma

While Delta tells you the immediate price change of a put option for a $1 move in the stock, Gamma focuses on how Delta itself changes with the stock price.

Delta provides a straightforward directional insight, whereas Gamma explains the speed of that directional change.

For instance, Delta may predict the price drop in a put as the stock price rises, while Gamma shows how this sensitivity lessens as the stock price moves further away from the strike price.

Practical Example

If a stock price increases by $1:

• A put with Delta = -0.50 and Gamma = 0.10 will see Delta shift from -0.50 to -0.40. This means the initial drop in the option price slows down as Delta adjusts due to Gamma.

Understanding both Delta and Gamma helps traders anticipate price changes more accurately and manage risks in a volatile market.

videos.title: How to Copy Trade Options - Stock Options Trading Course for Beginners
videos.description:
The prices of calls and puts are influenced by several factors, including the strike price, maturity (expiration), and the underlying asset’s price. Here’s a breakdown of how prices for calls and puts differ based on these factors:

1. Strike Price

• Calls: The price of a call option tends to rise as the strike price moves closer to the current price of the underlying asset, and further if it becomes “in the money” (when the underlying asset’s price is above the strike price). Calls gain more value as the stock price increases.

• Puts: Conversely, the price of a put option tends to rise as the strike price moves further above the current price of the underlying asset, becoming “in the money” when the stock price falls below the strike price. Puts gain more value as the stock price decreases.

2. Maturity (Expiration Date)

• Longer Maturity: Options with longer expiration dates typically have higher premiums because they give more time for the underlying asset’s price to move in a favorable direction. This holds true for both calls and puts.

• Shorter Maturity: Options with shorter expiration dates have lower premiums because there’s less time for the asset’s price to move. This makes them riskier and decreases their time value.

3. Volatility and Time Value

• Implied Volatility: Both calls and puts become more expensive as volatility increases. Higher volatility means there’s a greater chance the underlying stock will make a large price move, benefiting both calls and puts.

• Time Decay: As an option nears its expiration, its time value decreases (known as time decay). Shorter maturity options decay faster, especially if they are out of the money.

4. Comparing Calls vs Puts

• Calls: Typically more expensive when the underlying stock is trending upwards or when volatility is high, because they give the right to profit from price increases.

• Puts: Tend to be more expensive in a bearish market or when the underlying stock’s price is falling, as they allow the holder to profit from declines in stock prices.

Understanding the Order Book: Bid, Ask, and the Difference Between Limit and Market Orders

In this video, we’ll take a closer look at the order book, an essential tool for traders, and explain key concepts such as bid, ask, and the difference between limit and market orders.

• Order Book: The order book is a real-time list of buy and sell orders for a specific stock or asset. It shows the prices and quantities at which traders are willing to buy and sell. The order book provides insights into market sentiment and liquidity.

• Bid Price: This is the highest price a buyer is willing to pay for an asset. The bid represents the demand side of the market.

• Ask Price: The ask is the lowest price a seller is willing to accept for an asset. It represents the supply side of the market.

• Bid-Ask Spread: The difference between the bid and ask prices is called the bid-ask spread. A narrower spread typically indicates higher liquidity and a more efficient market, while a wider spread may suggest lower liquidity.

• Market Order: A market order is an instruction to buy or sell an asset immediately at the best available price. Market orders ensure that the trade will be executed right away, but the price at which the trade is executed can vary depending on the order book’s liquidity.

• Limit Order: A limit order is an order to buy or sell an asset at a specific price or better. With a limit order, you can control the price at which you are willing to trade, but there’s no guarantee that the order will be executed unless the market reaches your specified price.

In this video, we’ll guide you through how to read the order book, understand the bid and ask prices, and use limit and market orders effectively to enhance your trading strategies.

videos.title: How Pricey is your Option? Stock Option Breakeven Point - Stock Options for Beginners
videos.description:
Are you getting a deal? Or is your option expensive?

How Pricey is your Option?

A Quick Guide on How to Calculate the Call Option Breakeven Point and Required Stock Jump for Profit

In this video, we’ll walk you through how to calculate the breakeven point for a call option, and we’ll also show you how to figure out the required percentage stock jump needed for you to break even on your investment.

1. Breakeven Formula:

To find the breakeven point for a call option, use this formula:

Breakeven Point = Strike Price + Premium
• Strike Price: The price at which you have the right to buy the stock.
• Premium: The price you paid for the option.

For example:

• If you buy a call option with a strike price of $50 and a premium of $5, your breakeven point would be:

Breakeven Point = $50 (Strike) + $5 (Premium) = $55

This means that for you to break even, the stock price needs to rise to $55.

2. Calculating the Yield (Stock Jump) to Breakeven:

Now, let’s calculate the percentage the stock needs to jump for you to break even.

The formula to calculate the required percentage stock jump to reach breakeven is:

Breakeven % Yield = ((Strike + Premium) / Current Stock Price) - 1

This gives you the percentage increase required for the stock price to hit your breakeven point.

For example:
• Assume the current stock price is $52.
• The strike price is $50, and the premium is $5.

First, calculate the breakeven point:
Breakeven Point = $50 (Strike) + $5 (Premium) = $55

Then, plug it into the formula:

Breakeven % Yield = (($55) / $52) - 1 = 0.0577 or 5.77%

This means the stock needs to rise by 5.77% for you to break even.

3. Implied Volatility & Breakeven % Upside:

Wondering if that option is a steal or overpriced? Our app’s got you covered with a powerful feature—Implied Volatility (IV) signal and Breakeven % Upside analysis! 📊

1. Implied Volatility tells you how much the market thinks a stock will move.
The higher the IV, the pricier the option, because there’s a bigger chance it’ll end up profitable.

Our app compares the option’s IV between similar stocks and does it with its historical volatility as well, helping you instantly see if you’re getting a good deal or paying too much.

2. Check out how much the stock needs to rise if held until maturity just to breakeven! 📈 This is determined by analyzing the Strike Price and the Premium (the cost of your option).

Different stocks have different prices, so a $5 option on one stock might be a bargain (if the stock price is high), while on another, it could be a rip-off (if the stock price is low).

Breakeven % Upside = (Strike + Premium) / Current Stock Price

Our app compares the option’s Breakeven % upside between stocks, helping you instantly see if you’re getting a good deal or paying too much.

💡 Understanding Asset Classes & Risk

Every investment you make belongs to an asset class — a category of investment that behaves in a certain way.

Here are the main ones:

• Bonds (Fixed Income) – Lower risk, steady income. Less growth, but more stability.
• Cash & Savings – Lowest risk, but loses value over time due to inflation.
• Real Estate – Tangible and often stable, but less liquid and can be expensive to access.
• Stocks (Equities) – Medium risk, higher potential return. Great for long-term growth but volatile in the short term.
• Stock Options, Crypto & Alternatives – High Risk — can be profitable, but risky.

Why Diversification Matters

Diversification means not putting all your eggs in one basket. Different assets respond differently to economic events. When stocks fall, bonds might rise. When inflation rises, gold might protect your wealth.

The goal is to:
 • Reduce risk
 • Smooth out performance
 • Protect your portfolio in uncertain times

Think of it like building a team: you want fast players, strong defenders, and a goalkeeper — not 11 strikers.

What Is Market Risk & How to Stay Ahead

Market risk is the risk that impacts all investments - regardless of how great your stock pick is. 

It’s the broad, systemic risk tied to the economy, interest rates, inflation, and global events. 

You can’t avoid it completely, but you can understand it and manage exposure better.

One of the most important tools to measure market risk at the stock level is beta.
• Beta measures a stock’s sensitivity to the overall market (usually the S&P 500).
• A beta of 1 means the stock moves with the market.
• A beta above 1 means the stock is more volatile than the market.
• A beta below 1 means it’s less volatile — more defensive.

In the app, every stock includes its beta so you can gauge risk before entering a position.

But market risk is about more than just beta — it’s also driven by key macro events:
📅 CPI (Consumer Price Index): Measures inflation at the consumer level.
🏭 PPI (Producer Price Index): Measures inflation at the producer level.
🏦 FOMC (Federal Open Market Committee): Determines interest rates and monetary policy.
💼 Jobs reports, GDP releases, earnings seasons, and geopolitical news also play a huge role.

All these events can shake the market — even great stocks fall if the entire market panics.

That’s why the app includes a live event calendar so you know what’s coming and when to expect volatility.

We also give you access to our exclusive Market Calendar Yield feature — a tool that shows how the market has historically performed during specific weeks, months, and even days of the year.

This lets you:

With these tools — beta, event tracking, and historical yield patterns — you’ll be better equipped to navigate market risk.

Use them to stay informed, manage position sizes, and protect your capital during volatile times.

What Are Earnings & How to Trade Them

Earnings are a company’s official report card: they reveal how much money a company made (or lost) over the past quarter. 

Investors look at EPS (earnings per share), revenue, and guidance to assess growth, strength, and future potential.

Here are 4 proven strategies to profit from earnings:

1️⃣ Pre-Earnings Run-Up

Some stocks rise into earnings as anticipation builds. You can buy before the report and sell just before the announcement to capture the hype, avoiding the risk of surprises.

2️⃣ Earnings Jump

When a company beats expectations, the stock can gap up at the open. Traders can enter right after confirmation and ride momentum if volume and sentiment support it.

3️⃣ Post-Earnings Drift

Even after a big move, strong earnings often lead to continued upward drift over the next few weeks. Use this for swing trades after the dust settles.

4️⃣ Earnings vs. Competitors

Watch how a stock performs relative to its peers. If Microsoft beats and Google misses, the market often rewards the outperformer and punishes the laggard — that’s a chance to trade the spread.

In the app, you can track earnings dates, analyst expectations, and compare results across companies — so you’re ready for every phase of the earnings cycle.

How to profit from Earnings?

When a company reports earnings, investors look at three key components:

1. Income Statement

Shows revenue, expenses, and profit (net income) over a specific period. This is where EPS (earnings per share) comes from — a major market mover.

2. Balance Sheet

A snapshot of what the company owns (assets) and owes (liabilities). It shows financial health, debt levels, and cash reserves.

3. Earnings Guidance

Arguably the most important for stock movement. 

This is management’s forecast for future revenue and profit. Even if a company beats earnings, weak guidance can make the stock drop — and vice versa.


 How Stocks React on Earnings Day:
• Beat + Strong Guidance → stock often jumps
• Beat + Weak Guidance → mixed or negative reaction
• Miss + Strong Guidance → recovery potential
• Miss + Weak Guidance → likely drop

videos.title: 13) Corporate Actions = Trading Opportunity | Dividend Announcement, Stock Split, Buy Back, Mergers
videos.description:
Corporate Actions: Trading Opportunity

Corporate actions often create short-term hype — and in the app, you receive signals to spot and trade these opportunities before the crowd. Here’s how each corporate event can affect a stock:

⸻

Dividend Announcement

When a company declares a dividend, it signals financial strength.
• Effect: Short-term price bump (especially with high yield), followed by a dip on the ex-div date.
• Opportunity: Profit by entering before the announcement or selling into yield-chasing demand.

⸻

Stock Split

The company increases share count, lowering the price per share.
• Effect: Often bullish, as it improves affordability and attracts retail traders.
• Opportunity: Ride momentum leading up to the split date — especially for popular tech names.

⸻

Merger & Acquisition

One company buys another or two combine.
• Effect: The target stock usually surges, while the buyer may drop slightly.
• Opportunity: Trade the target on the initial spike or find sympathy plays in the same sector.

⸻

Share Buyback

The company repurchases its own shares, reducing supply.
• Effect: Often boosts stock price and earnings per share.
• Opportunity: Bullish signal — can be used to confirm long entries or add to a position.

⸻

Private Placement

Shares are sold to a select group, usually at a discount.
• Effect: Can dilute existing shareholders, leading to short-term drops.
• Opportunity: Wait for dip buying or enter when placement terms are favorable.

⸻

In the app, you’ll get alerts when these events occur — with breakdowns, impact scores, and how to trade them.
